title: Deer Trail Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Deer Trail wells have a median depth of 212 feet, with local drilling and completed-well cost ranges for rural buyers.
h1: Deer Trail, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land near Deer Trail means understanding the well record before you rely on a listing’s water claim. Within 5 miles, Colorado DWR records show 375 permitted wells, including 217 recorded as constructed. Depth, production, and water levels vary substantially across this plains area.

The records point to Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, with permits naming fractured-bedrock, Laramie Fox Hills, and alluvial aquifers. Use these figures to budget a new well, compare nearby properties, and identify questions for a driller before closing.

sections.heading: Deer Trail well depths vary sharply across the plains
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Deer Trail is 212 feet. The middle half runs from 41 to 360 feet, which is a wide spread for a drilling estimate. The 90th percentile is 420 feet, and the deepest record reaches 660 feet.

Depth mix matters when you read a driller’s bid. Forty-eight percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 41% fall between 300 and 600 feet. Only 10% are between 100 and 300 feet, and 2% reach beyond 600 feet. That distribution means a nearby shallow well does not guarantee a shallow hole on your parcel.

Permits identify Denver Basin aquifers in 100% of the records. Named formations include the Laramie Fox Hills and alluvial units, but many permits refer to unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. Ask for nearby well logs, not just an advertised average.

sections.heading: Most Deer Trail wells report usable production
sections.html:
Among the 109 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Fifty-eight percent are in the 5-to-15-gallon-per-minute range, and 33% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

No recorded well in this dataset falls under 1 gallon per minute. Still, 9% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, so a buyer should not treat the median as a guarantee for every lot. Yield testing, storage capacity, and the intended household or livestock use all matter.

Use mix is part of the context: 43% of permits are for stock use, 39% domestic or household, and 14% irrigation. A stock or irrigation well record may not tell you what a domestic well on your property will produce.

sections.heading: Deer Trail water levels show a deeper recent reading
sections.html:
Only 33 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is much smaller than the depth record. The median depth to water is 34 feet, with the middle half from 27 to 161 feet below the surface.

The decade comparison deserves attention. The median static water level was 32 feet below surface in the 2000s and 135 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper recent reading in this permit sample, but it is not enough by itself to prove a uniform regional decline. Different wells, aquifers, locations, and measurement conditions can affect the result.

Before buying near Deer Trail, Peoria, or Strasburg, compare static levels and construction details from wells closest to the parcel. A local driller can also explain whether the proposed site is likely to encounter the same water-bearing interval.

sections.heading: Deer Trail permit history shows continuing drilling
sections.html:
Deer Trail has a long permit history. Records show 7 permits from the 1950s, 25 from the 1960s, 33 from the 1970s, 25 from the 1980s, 53 from the 1990s, 71 from the 2000s, 53 from the 2010s, and 36 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active driller names in the records are Don Eastwood Drilling Inc., listed as Eastwood, Don, with 59 wells; Hamacher Well Works Inc., listed as Hamacher, Alan Ray, with 32; and Authorized, listed as Pe, Pg, with 31.

These records show who has worked in the area, but they do not guarantee availability, price, or performance on a new job. Verify the current license, scope of work, casing and grout details, pump selection, testing, and permit responsibilities before signing.

sections.heading: A median-depth Deer Trail well can cost this much
sections.html:
The local cost model uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 212-foot median depth, the drilled hole calculates to about $10,600 to $14,900.

A finished well costs more than the hole. With a pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work included, the estimated total at the median depth is $16,600 to $26,900. Treat that as a planning range, not a fixed bid. Actual cost can change with depth, access, casing and grout requirements, power distance, site conditions, and the selected equipment.

The wide local depth range is the main budgeting warning. A property requiring 360, 420, or 660 feet can be materially different from one with a shallow hole. Get a written estimate that separates drilling from completion and identifies what happens if the first target does not produce.

sections.heading: What Deer Trail buyers should check before building
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only risk. The records include 12 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. There are 0 historic mine features in that mapped area, but buyers should still test existing well water and review environmental information for the specific parcel.

Ask for the DWR permit, well construction report, pump test, static water level, treatment history, and recent laboratory results. Confirm that the well’s permitted use matches the planned house, livestock, or irrigation use. A well serving a new home also needs adequate separation from septic components and room for access, repair, and future replacement.

For a vacant lot, check water-rights requirements, augmentation needs in an over-appropriated basin, septic suitability, driveway access, electrical service, and building placement before closing. In fractured or variable formations, a dry hole or weak production is possible even when nearby wells look good.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Deer Trail, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth near Deer Trail is 212 feet. The middle half ranges from 41 to 360 feet, while the 90th percentile is 420 feet and the deepest record is 660 feet. Depth varies sharply: 48% of records are under 100 feet, while 41% are between 300 and 600 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Deer Trail?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 212-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $10,600 to $14,900. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $16,600 to $26,900. A deeper-than-median hole can cost substantially more.

faq.q: How much water do Deer Trail wells produce?
faq.a: Among 109 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Fifty-eight percent produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 33% report more than 15. Nine percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Deer Trail?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. There are 12 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the individual well through a qualified laboratory, review its history, and retest after ownership changes or suspected contamination.

faq.q: Are Deer Trail well water levels getting lower?
faq.a: The available water-level sample is limited to 33 wells. Median static water level was 32 feet below surface in the 2000s and 135 feet in the 2020s, showing a deeper recent reading. That comparison does not prove a uniform decline because wells, aquifers, locations, and measurement conditions differ.
